title: RPKI now protects 70% of internet routes (ipinfo.io)
comments: My concern about RPKI is legal pressure on the registries. By centralising all of Russia's allowed routes on a database server in the Netherlands and automatically enforcing it, it's trivial for the Dutch government to cut off Russia's internet access by tampering with that database.reply

Without RPKI, it would be easy for many governments to cut off Russia's internet access by launching a BGP attack.Assuming the Netherlands was acting unnilaterally, Russian ISPs would be able to coordinate with other ISPs to get back online via other routes. Assuming Russia's enemy wanted to press the issue, it would quickly devolve into a political question of who wants to allow Russian peering, who does not, and who is willing to not peer with peers of Russia (and peers of peers, etc).This has always been the case. The internet is a network of networks; all of which are subject to control by their host governments should they choose to exercise it. With or without RPKI, a partitioning of the Internet for a significant period of time was always going to be a political decision.reply

These routing announcements have historically depended heavily on trust. When a network announces addresses it shouldn’t, accidentally or deliberately, traffic can be sent to the wrong place and services can become unreachable.On February 24, 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) tried to block YouTube inside Pakistan by announcing a more specific route for YouTube's addresses. title: BIPM decides to stop adding leap seconds to UTC (bipm.org)
comments: Context: BIPM is responsible for the UTC time standard, and in this document they decide to stop adding (or removing) leap seconds, starting on 20th of May 2027 and lasting for the foreseeable future (until one leap hour is needed, but even then it's unclear if they'll do something). Together with the decision to not add a leap second in December, the 27 leap seconds that have been added so far should be the only ones, ever.The page lists several good reasons for this, including:- It's a common source of bugs.- Solar time is not that important in a world of coarse timezones.- IoT and anything that cannot receive time updates have trouble with leap seconds.- Negative leap seconds have never occurred before, but might occur in the future, and almost no software has tested this case.I'd also add:- Unix timestamps are actually defined as "seconds since epoch minus however many leap seconds have happened". It's a hack to keep code that assumes "86400 seconds in a day" from breaking. It means that during a leap second the Unix timestamp goes back and repeats a previous value, making them ambiguous and non-monotonic.- Leap second unpredictability can make it impossible to calculate how many seconds are between two UTC dates or Unix timestamps, for example the countdown to the year 2038 bug.- The proper ISO8601 formatting of leap seconds ("23:59:60") is widely unsupported, breaking parsers, along with the assumption of how many seconds are in a minute, hour, or day.---EDIT: I've emailed hn@ycombinator.com to change the title. It's avoiding editorialization, but I think it's also preventing the post from getting the attention it deserves.I'm booking a yearly one-second-long holiday on my calendar, to celebrate all the headaches this will save me. Happy end of leap seconds!reply

So it's kinda a joke to even talk about leap hours. I'm shocked they're even mentioning such an idea, they should have declared it as a non-solution.reply

title: Non-Determinism Doesn't Matter (sklar.rocks)
comments: When people refute the idea that "LLM is the new compiler from natural language to code" the common reason is that LLM is non-deterministic but compiler is deterministic.But the determinism isn't the real distinction. LLM inference can be made deterministic (temparaute zero, etc.). And multi-threaded compiler can be non-dterministic.And human developers are also non-deterministic. There is always the nondeterminism even before AI.I think the real difference is how leaky the abstraction is. If you just need to understand language instead of compiler internal to write correct code, the compiler is non-leaky abstrction. If you rely on compiler to do auto SIMD optimization, and have to do hacks to trigger the optimization, compiler is leaky abstraction.For AI, if you don't ever need to read the code and AI writes perfectly bug-free program that perfectly follows instruction, then AI is a non-leaky abstraction, but that's not the case for now. To make code maintainable and debuggable you still need to read the code if the project is complex enough.reply

> And human developers are also non-deterministic. There is always the nondeterminism even before AI.Pointing out humans are not deterministic is irrelevant to the comparison. In the original example of LLMs replacing compilers, the deterministic compiler is being replaced, not the non-deterministic human. In the original example, we move from non-deterministic human -> sourced code -> deterministic compiler, to non-deterministic human -> sourced prompt(?) -> non-deterministic LLM. The important part is the sourced code into a deterministic final step so your build artifact doesn't change.You can point out you can change temperature to zero or what ever, but then you don't actually get the build artifact you wanted in the first place.reply

Yeah, it's not the non-determinism; it's that they don't do what I say. I can't imagine writing a nontrivial program without, at a minimum, reading and editing the pieces as they're being produced. People aren't complaining about non-determinism; they're complaining about the results being non-deterministically sometimes wrong.reply

> I think the real difference is how leaky the abstraction is. If you just need to understand language instead of compiler internal to write correct code, the compiler is non-leaky abstrction. If you rely on compiler to do auto SIMD optimization, and have to do hacks to trigger the optimization, compiler is leaky abstraction.Autovectorization is not a programming model!I forgot who put me on that article - I think it might've been Horace He - but that is a pretty big idea in idea space for me.reply

> LLMs, and their respective harnesses, are actors in a system. Code is just an output.This tracks well with my experiences integrating AI into a software dev pipeline. Sure the output of an LLM is not deterministic in the same sense as a compiler (at least when the LLM has the typical configuration). However, that just means the LLM should not be solely responsible for the final product of your pipeline.reply

I'm so tired of the endless stream of articles that a.) don't know what "non-determinism" means in Computer Science and b.) don't really understand how LLMs work."Non-determinism" (i.e. the "N" in NP-Complete) does not mean "random", it means "following all paths at once" (there's a really elegant way to understand the List monad as representing non-deterministic computing). It's such a fundamental (and delightful) concept in computer science that refusing to understand what it means is a tragedy related to the loss of technical language itself.But, even if we just sub "non-deterministic" for "inconsistent" or "random" or "stochastic" or whatever better term you come up with. Statements like the following just seem to not understand the basic architecture of LLMs:> Given the same input prompt, a model's output is not guaranteed to be identical on every run, at least under normal running conditions."Normal running conditions"? The reproducibility of the output is 100% a property of how you choose to sample from an LLM. There are virtually endless ways you can define your sampler and whether or not the same result is reproducible is a fairly minor aspect of all the other choices you make when sampling.At the end of the day, each step of the LLM gives you a distribution over next tokens, and you can do with that what you like.In the end the article almost becomes a tautology: the output of an LLM represents a probability distribution over all the outputs it believes are valid with some variation around an expected output. Yes, that's literally what an LLM is.reply

> One of my fundamental objections to LLM-driven software development was that model output is non-deterministic.Model outputs are deterministic. Your API provider may be injecting untunable amounts of randomness, but if you're not at the whim of an opaque cloud service, your model can be as deterministic as you please.The unease that you describe isn't about models not being deterministic (because they are), it's that generating outputs from LLMs is an inherently inductive process (operating backwards by extrapolating from observations and examples) rather than a deductive process (operating forwards from careful logical reasoning founded on axiomatic principles). Deductive processes are more reliable, predictable, and analyzable than inductive processes, but they're also much harder to produce for many classes of problems.reply
first_paragraph: One of my fundamental objections to LLM-driven software development was that model output is non-deterministic. Given the same input prompt, a model's output is not guaranteed to be identical on every run, at least under normal running conditions.I used to think that this was a severe limitation of AI tools. How could we possibly use this unpredictable building block to craft systems that require precise and exact calculations?But as I started to get more comfortable running AI as my primary means of "writing" code, I had a revelation:While the result needs to be exact, there is not one correct way to get there. The means by which you obtain a correct result do not need to be deterministic!Previously, I was used to specifying behavior in terms of code: precise sets of instructions that compile and execute in a predictable way. And mentally, I was treating LLM output like code. But over time, I realized that LLMs play a fundamentally different role than code does in software engineering

The conference paper is pp. 125-135 https://archive.org/details/historyofcomputi0000inte/page/12... in A History of Computing in the Twentieth Century (1980, Metropolis, Howlett and Rota eds., ISBN 0-12-491650-3 ). Naturally it also got a session at the first History of Programming Languages conference in 1978 https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/960118.808379 at which Backus spoke again https://dl.acm.org/doi/book/10.1145/800025#sec2 . I used to work on software that still uses Fortran from the 50's and is still in maintenance and use today. IIRC, it had ~700kloc of Fortran. It may be the oldest and largest Fortran codebase still in use.My first project there was removing all of the Hollerith from the code. Since Fortran predated strings, you had to manipulate them as integers. When you tied that to the original Fortran dynamic memory system, Dynosour, which used equivalenced arrays as pointers, it was a disaster.It also gave me an appreciation for JavaBeanFactoryFactory. The original Fortran limited identifiers to six characters, the first of which indicated whether the variable was an integer, logical (bool), or real (float). I will take a 100 character name over ILBNK1 every single time.GOTOs were surprisingly not a big problem, but structured code is definitely a bit easier to read, especially since it brought the practice of indentation with it.Overall, it was a great experience but I wouldn't want to do it again, even if the work was interesting.reply
